item.title: Medicare: Out-of-Pocket Costs and Other Factors Can Affect Use of Services for Cardiovascular Disease Prevention
item.description:
What GAO Found
Medicare covers two types of services for cardiovascular disease prevention: Medicare preventive services and medically necessary services. Specifically, five Medicare preventive services are covered that aim to prevent the onset of cardiovascular disease or identify it early. Two such services are cardiovascular behavioral therapy to reduce disease risk and lipid panels to screen for the disease.Medically necessary services are to diagnose or treat conditions that are cardiovascular disease risk factors and prevent disease progression. Two examples include cardiac rehabilitation, which aims to improve cardiac health through a program of supervised exercise and behavioral counseling, and lipid panels to monitor high cholesterol levels.
Examples of Services for Cardiovascular Disease Prevention
Note: For more details, see figures 2 and 3 in GAO-27-108423.
Out-of-pocket costs can affect beneficiaries’ use of specific services for cardiovascular disease prevention, according to representatives GAO interviewed from eight stakeholder organizations. For example, because cardiac rehabilitation typically takes place over 36 sessions, even modest cost-sharing amounts can accumulate, according to a representative from one provider organization. Research also has found that beneficiaries with higher out-of-pocket costs were more likely to discontinue rehabilitation sessions or prescribed medication. In addition, representatives mentioned that patient factors and provider availability can also affect beneficiaries’ use of these services.
About 90 percent of beneficiaries with traditional Medicare in GAO’s analysis (16.2 million out of 18.1 million) received at least one lipid test from 2021 through 2025, according to Medicare claims data. During that period, beneficiaries received just under 1.3 million lipid tests as Medicare preventive services and 91.6 million as medically necessary services. Relatively few beneficiaries had claims in 2025 for cardiovascular behavioral therapy and the other selected services analyzed by GAO. This may be due to providers’ lack of awareness of these services’ coverage or because they delivered similar services but did not bill these specific codes, as described by representatives from stakeholder organizations.
Why GAO Did This Study
Cardiovascular disease—which includes coronary heart disease, stroke, and other conditions affecting the heart and blood vessels—has been the leading cause of death for adults in the U.S. for over 100 years. The prevalence of risk factors for cardiovascular disease is highest among older adults, the main population covered by Medicare.
GAO was asked to review issues related to beneficiaries’ use of health services for cardiovascular disease prevention. This report describes (1) services covered by Medicare for cardiovascular disease prevention, (2) key factors affecting beneficiaries’ use of services, and (3) beneficiaries’ use of selected services for cardiovascular disease prevention in traditional Medicare.
GAO reviewed clinical guidelines and recommendations, agency documentation, and applicable laws and regulations. GAO analyzed claims and beneficiary enrollment data to identify the proportion of beneficiaries with claims for four selected services for cardiovascular disease prevention, including lipid testing and cardiovascular behavioral therapy to reduce disease risk. To align with certain Medicare coverage provisions, GAO analyzed claims from 2021 through 2025 (the most recent year available) for lipid testing and claims from 2025 for the three other selected services.
GAO also interviewed agency officials and representatives from nine stakeholder organizations representing health care providers and researchers, and Medicare beneficiaries. To supplement the interviews, GAO conducted a literature search of selected research about factors affecting beneficiaries’ use of services for cardiovascular disease prevention.
For more information, contact Leslie V. Gordon at GordonLV@gao.gov.
